n: Satan incites David to count Israel’s fighting men. The parallel in 2 Samuel says the Lord “moved” David; the chronicler makes clear that the tempter was Satan, while God permitted the test.

f.g: Hebrew “adversary” or “accuser.” This is one of the few Old Testament passages to use it as a proper name.
Take a military census—probably reflecting pride in his own strength rather than trust in God.

n: David orders Joab and the leaders to count everyone from Beer-sheba in the south to Dan in the north, so that he can know his total strength.

f.g: From one end of the land to the other.
The motive seems to be pride—David wanted to measure his power.

n: Joab objects: may God multiply the people a hundredfold, but why do this? Why bring guilt on Israel? Even the hard-nosed general senses that this is wrong.

f.g: A reason for guilt to fall on the nation.

f.w: an hundred times so many more

n: David overrules Joab, who reluctantly carries out the census throughout Israel.

f.w: the king's word prevailed against Joab

n: Joab reports 1,100,000 fighting men in Israel and 470,000 in Judah. The numbers differ from 2 Samuel, perhaps because of different counting methods or copying.

f.w: a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand
f.g: 1,100,000; 2 Samuel 24:9 gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah.
Able to fight.

n: Joab is so disgusted by the order that he leaves out Levi and Benjamin. Levi was exempt from military service by law, and Benjamin’s territory included the tabernacle at Gibeon.

f.g: Detestable; repugnant.

f.w: Levi and Benjamin counted he not

n: God is displeased and strikes Israel. A leader’s pride can bring consequences on many people.

f.w: God was displeased with this thing

n: David’s conscience awakens. He confesses honestly, asks God to take away his guilt, and admits he acted foolishly. Quick, sincere repentance marks David at his best.

f.g: Remove the guilt; forgive the sin.

n: The Lord speaks to Gad, David’s prophet.

f.g: A prophet who “sees” by revelation.

n: Gad brings David a choice of three consequences.

f.g: God lets David choose the form of the consequence.

n: Gad delivers the Lord’s message.

f.g: Choose for yourself.

n: The options: three years of famine, three months of military defeat, or three days of plague from the Lord’s angel.

f.g: 2 Samuel 24:13 reads seven years; the three-three-three pattern here may be original.
Plague; deadly epidemic disease.
Think it over and decide.

n: David chooses to fall into the Lord’s hands rather than man’s, because God’s mercies are great. Even in judgment, he trusts God’s character.

f.w: I am in a great strait
f.g: I am in great distress; a terrible dilemma.

f.w: for very great are his mercies

n: The plague strikes, and seventy thousand Israelites die.
As the angel prepares to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord relents and says, “Enough!” The angel stops beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. God’s mercy limits His judgments.

f.w: he repented him of the evil
f.g: He relented from the disaster—a human way of describing God’s mercy, not a change of character.
Called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24:16.

n: David sees the angel between heaven and earth with a drawn sword over Jerusalem. He and the elders, wearing sackcloth, fall face down in humility.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of mourning and repentance.

n: David takes full responsibility: I sinned, not these sheep. Let the punishment fall on me and my family, not on the people. Like a true shepherd, he offers himself for his flock—a faint foreshadowing of Christ.

f.w: these sheep, what have they done?
be on me, and on my father's house
f.g: David asks that the punishment fall on himself and his own family instead of the nation.

n: Through Gad, the angel instructs David to build an altar at Ornan’s threshing floor. The place of judgment becomes the place of worship.

f.w: set up an altar unto the LORD

n: David obeys immediately, following the prophet’s word.

f.g: In obedience to the prophet’s message.

n: Ornan, threshing wheat, sees the angel; his four sons hide in fear.

f.g: Separating grain from stalks, done on high, open ground to catch the wind.

n: When the king arrives, Ornan bows to the ground before him.

f.w: bowed himself to David with his face to the ground
f.g: A sign of deep respect to a king.

n: David asks to buy the threshing floor at full price so he can build an altar and stop the plague.
Ornan generously offers it all for free—land, oxen for sacrifice, threshing sledges for firewood, and wheat for the grain offering.

f.g: The grain offering; “meat” in the KJV means food in general.
Wooden sledges dragged over grain to thresh it.

n: David refuses: “I will not… offer burnt offerings without cost.” True sacrifice to God must cost us something.

f.w: nor offer burnt offerings without cost

n: David pays 600 shekels of gold for the site. 2 Samuel records fifty shekels of silver—perhaps for the threshing floor alone, while Chronicles gives the price of the whole hilltop.

f.g: About 15 pounds (7 kg) of gold.

n: David builds the altar and offers sacrifices, and God answers with fire from heaven—the same sign that approved the tabernacle and later the temple.

f.w: he answered him from heaven by fire

n: The Lord commands the angel to sheathe his sword. Through repentance and sacrifice, the judgment ends.

f.w: he put up his sword again into the sheath
f.g: The judgment is finished.

n: Seeing that God accepted his offering there, David continues to sacrifice at this site.

f.g: God’s acceptance marked this as a holy place.

n: The old tabernacle and its altar were still at Gibeon, the official place of sacrifice at the time.
But David was afraid to travel to Gibeon because of the angel’s sword. This explains why Ornan’s threshing floor—Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac—became the site of Solomon’s temple.

f.w: the sword of the angel of the LORD
